item.title: Best Phone Pouches That Block Wi-Fi and Cellular Signals
item.dc:creator: Brett Kleinberg
item.description: Compare phone pouches that block Wi-Fi and cellular signals on shielding, locking, rollout support, and pricing model for schools, exams, and courts.
item.content:encoded:
Every signal-blocking pouch makes the same basic promise: put a phone inside, and calls, texts, notifications, and data stop reaching it. But the people buying these pouches want very different things from them. A traveler or privacy-minded owner wants a sleeve they control, one they can seal when it matters and open the moment it doesn’t. A school, testing center, or courthouse wants the opposite: hundreds of phones silenced at once, and confidence that none of them come out until someone in charge decides they should.

This ranking is written mainly for institutions, with notes for individual buyers where their needs differ. We judged each of the five brands on how well it blocks signals and whether the maker has published testing to prove it, whether the pouch locks and who holds the key, what kind of support the company provides, and how it sells the product.

Do You Need Signal Blocking, a Lock, or Both?

Locking a phone away and blocking its signal solve two different problems. A locking pouch keeps the phone out of someone’s hands; a signal-blocking pouch keeps the phone itself silent and offline. Many phone-free schools need only the first. Once a student can’t reach their phone, it has already stopped being a distraction, whether or not it’s still receiving texts.

Organizations that need signal blocking usually have a specific reason:

  • An RFP, district policy, or exam rule requires it.

  • Stored phones keep buzzing and chiming, and the noise is disrupting the room.

  • Students are hotspotting a phone to a laptop, or screen mirroring, to reach sites the school network blocks.

  • A court needs to keep jurors and witnesses from receiving outside messages or looking up information about the case during proceedings.

  • The setting is an exam, a hearing, or a confidential meeting, where a connected device is a risk even when nobody is holding it.

Airplane mode won’t cover these cases. For one thing, it relies on every single person turning it on and leaving it on. For another, NIST’s guidance on mobile device forensics notes that airplane mode doesn’t always shut off services such as GPS. A shielded pouch works the same way no matter how the phone is set, as long as it’s fully closed, since any gap in the closure lets signal through.

Evaluation Criteria

Criteria What We Evaluate
Signal blocking and disclosure Which signals the pouch blocks and what the maker publishes about testing. A test of the finished pouch against a named standard tells a buyer more than a claim about the fabric.
Closure and access control Whether the pouch locks, who can open it, and whether staff can tell if someone tried. With a roll-top or Velcro closure, that decision belongs to the person carrying it.
Use at scale Whether the pouch is built and supported for hundreds of people at once, with unlocking equipment and a check-in routine.
Implementation and program support What the vendor provides beyond hardware, such as policy help, training, launch support, and ongoing troubleshooting.
Pricing model Whether the price is one-time or recurring, and what it includes beyond the pouch itself.

Overall Ranking

Ranked based on qualitative performance across the five criteria above.

Rank Brand Signal Blocking Closure and Access Use at Scale Program Support Pricing Model

2 Disklabs Faraday bags built for police and forensic work Sleeve closure; lockable version seals with a clip for evidence tags Police, forensic, and corporate security teams Product-focused; no rollout program identified Per-unit purchase
3 Faraday Defense Layered Faraday fabric with published fabric shielding figures Roll-top with Velcro or magnetic double fold; does not lock Military, police, and forensic buyers; bulk school orders Product-focused; bulk and custom color orders Per-unit purchase
4 QuietCase Lockable signal-blocking pouch Zip-lock mechanism; school version opens at a QuietBase Schools in the US and UK Rollout kit and staff onboarding support Education pricing, no subscription
5 UZBL HDDN Faraday sleeve for cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth Velcro; opened by the student K-12 classrooms Sold through education procurement channels Per-unit, volume pricing

Brand Overviews

Yondr

Yondr’s Faraday pouch blocks signal and locks securely, opening only at a universal unlocking station. It’s one of three pouches in Yondr’s lineup, alongside a standard locking pouch that doesn’t block signal and a Velcro pouch for people who need quick access to their phone for medical reasons. Because buyers choose signal blocking when they order, a school or agency can match each pouch to the room it’s used in and skip shielding where it isn’t needed.

Yondr signal-blocking pouches are deployed in schools, courthouses, university testing centers, corporate offices and worksites, and standardized testing environments including bar and civil service exams. For a look at how that runs day to day, Purdue Testing Services publishes its routine. Each test-taker's phone, smartwatch, and earbuds go into a Yondr pouch, a proctor locks it at check-in, and the pouch stays on the desk until check-out.

The lock is a proprietary pushpin design and it's tamper-evident, so staff can tell when a pouch has been opened, and people hold on to their own phone the whole time. The program around the pouch covers policy consultation, operational planning, training, launch support, and a partner success contact, and it draws on more than a decade of rollouts. Yondr is sold as a one-time purchase with volume-based pricing, and what Yondr costs in 2026 explains what that price includes.

  • How it blocks signal: Faraday signal-blocking configuration; standard non-blocking pouch also available

  • How it closes: Proprietary pushpin lock, tamper-evident; opened at an unlocking base

  • Beyond the product: Policy consultation, training, launch support, ongoing partner success support

  • Who it suits: Schools, testing centers, courts, and workplaces that need phones both silent and secured, with help running the rollout

Summary of Online Reviews
Testing directors describe the change in plain terms: "phones and cheating were always an issue, but since using Yondr, we have had zero incidents." A law school dean called the rollout "a night and day transformation," citing "consistency, security, and a clear message of integrity." Teachers put it more simply: "I feel like I have a chance as a teacher now."

Disklabs

Disklabs is a digital forensics company in the UK, and its Faraday bags are made for police forces, forensic teams, and corporate security departments. The Phone Shield bags are sold as police approved under the UK's Secured by Design scheme. They're built to cut a seized or sensitive device off from mobile networks, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth, and there's a lockable Phone Shield version that closes with a clip so the bag can be sealed with evidence tags. Disklabs doesn't publish a rollout or training program for schools or testing centers.

  • How it blocks signal: Faraday shielding built for forensic evidence handling

  • How it closes: Sleeve closure; lockable version seals with a clip for evidence tags

  • Beyond the product: Product-focused; no rollout or training program identified

  • Who it suits: Investigators and security teams shielding individual devices

Summary of Online Reviews
Investigators and security teams say “the bag works as described,” and several add that it “blocks signal better than the cheaper bags we tried first.” Some note “it’s built for one device at a time, not a room full of them.”

Faraday Defense

Faraday Defense is a US company selling Faraday bags, fabric, and enclosures to military, police, and forensic buyers, and to consumers as well. Its phone bags are made of layered Faraday fabric, and the company publishes shielding figures for that fabric. They close with either a double roll and Velcro or a magnetic double fold. None of them lock, which leaves it to the person carrying the bag to decide when it opens. Schools can place bulk orders and choose custom colors.

  • How it blocks signal: Layered Faraday fabric; shielding figures published for the fabric

  • How it closes: Double roll with Velcro, or magnetic double fold; no lock

  • Beyond the product: Bulk orders and custom colors; no rollout or training program identified

  • Who it suits: Individuals and security teams that want a shielded bag they open themselves

Summary of Online Reviews
Verified buyers report that “signal drops as soon as the bag is sealed,” with one noting “it cut out after the first fold.” The trade-off mentioned most is size: “I wish it were small enough to fit in a pocket.”

QuietCase

QuietCase makes a lockable, signal-blocking phone pouch that it sells to families and to schools in the US and UK. The pouch closes with a zip lock. On the school version, a dedicated unlocking unit called the QuietBase opens it. Along with the hardware, QuietCase provides a rollout kit, a demo kit, and staff onboarding support, and its education pricing carries no subscription.

  • How it blocks signal: Signal-blocking pouch construction

  • How it closes: Zip-lock mechanism; school version opens at a QuietBase

  • Beyond the product: Rollout kit, demo kit, and staff onboarding support

  • Who it suits: Schools that want a lockable signal-blocking pouch with starter rollout materials

Summary of Online Reviews
Schools point to “a rollout kit that made the first week easier,” and to “onboarding support that answered our staff’s questions.” A few mention delivery delays, including “an order that arrived weeks after the promised date.”

UZBL HDDN

UZBL makes protective cases for school devices. HDDN is its Faraday sleeve for student phones; it blocks cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth signals and has a slot for an ID. The closure is Velcro, and UZBL presents that as a feature, since students can get to their phones without unlocking stations or help from staff. HDDN is sold with volume pricing, including through education resellers a school may already be buying from.

  • How it blocks signal: Faraday sleeve blocking cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth

  • How it closes: Velcro; opened by the student

  • Beyond the product: Volume pricing and availability through education resellers

  • Who it suits: Classrooms that want notifications silenced and are comfortable with student-controlled access

Summary of Online Reviews
IT teams mention that “ordering through our usual education reseller kept it simple,” and that “the ID slot helps keep track of whose sleeve is whose.” Some note “students can open the Velcro themselves, so it works more as a reminder than a lock.”

Subcategory Rankings

To show where each brand leads, the field is also broken into three narrower subcategories: blocking and locking together, rollout and program support, and shielding pedigree.

Best for Blocking and Locking Together

Rank Brand Why
1 Yondr Faraday configuration paired with a tamper-evident pushpin lock and staff-controlled unlocking bases
2 QuietCase Signal-blocking pouch with a zip-lock mechanism and school unlocking unit
3 Disklabs Lockable Phone Shield version seals with a clip for evidence tags

Best for Rollout and Program Support

Rank Brand Why
1 Yondr Policy consultation, training, launch support, and ongoing partner success support across 10+ years of rollouts
2 QuietCase Rollout kit, demo kit, and staff onboarding support for schools
3 UZBL HDDN Available through education resellers, which simplifies purchasing

Best for Shielding Pedigree

Rank Brand Why
1 Disklabs Police-approved Faraday bags from a digital forensics company
2 Yondr Signal-blocking pouches deployed in courthouses, testing centers, and bar and civil service exams
3 Faraday Defense Publishes shielding figures for the Faraday fabric used in its bags

Which Signal-Blocking Pouch Is Right for You?

If you're one person who wants a phone offline on demand, go to a Faraday specialist such as Disklabs or Faraday Defense, since a sleeve you can open yourself is the whole point.

A school, a testing center, a court, or a workplace needs a pouch that blocks signal and stays closed until staff open it, along with a rollout that people are still following after the first month, and Yondr is the entry here built around that combination.

Schools comparing K-12 options specifically can go deeper in our ranking of the best signal-blocking phone pouches for schools.

Talk to Yondr about the signal-blocking configuration for your school, testing center, or organization.

FAQs

Do signal-blocking pouches block both Wi-Fi and cellular?

Yes. A Faraday pouch wraps the phone in conductive material that blocks radio signals going in and coming out, and that covers cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and NFC. Pay as much attention to the seal as to the fabric, though, because shielding only works when the pouch is fully closed.

Is a signal-blocking pouch the same as a signal jammer?

No. A jammer transmits radio energy that disrupts other people's devices, and the FCC states that federal law prohibits operating, marketing, or selling jamming equipment, with no exemption for classrooms. A pouch transmits nothing and only shields the phone inside it.

Does Yondr sell a signal-blocking pouch?

Yes. Yondr offers a Faraday signal-blocking pouch with a secure lock and a universal unlocking station, and it also sells its standard pouch, which locks but doesn't block signal. Buyers choose the configuration when they order, and the same implementation program comes with either.

Methodology

This ranking reflects research conducted in October 2026, comparing five phone pouches that block Wi-Fi and cellular signals against five criteria: signal blocking and disclosure, closure and access control, use at scale, implementation and program support, and pricing model. Each brand was assessed from its own product pages, testing claims, and support materials, along with public customer feedback where it exists. Ratings are qualitative, applied the same way to every brand, and not combined into a composite score. Review summaries draw on published testimonials, public feedback, and recurring themes in vendor materials. Product details, testing disclosures, and pricing change often, so confirm current specifications with each vendor before buying.

item.title: Best Phone-Free Solutions for Comedy Shows
item.dc:creator: Brett Kleinberg
item.description: Compare phone-free solutions for comedy shows, from locking pouches to camera stickers, on protecting new material, club setup, and tour support.
item.content:encoded:
Comedians spend months working a new hour in clubs before anyone films it, and a shaky clip posted from the third row can spend a punchline for everyone who hasn't seen the show yet. That's a big part of why so many comedians have gone phone-free, and why the method matters so much in a comedy room.

This ranking compares five options for comedians, tour managers, and club owners, looking at how well each protects material, how it suits rooms of different sizes, what the night is like for the audience, who staffs it, and whether it can follow a comedian from one city to the next.

Does a Comedy Show Need Phones Locked Away?

Some rooms get by on a host's announcement and a door staff that pays attention. The shows that need more than that tend to have a few things in common:

  • New material is being worked out, and it isn't ready to be judged from a clip.

  • A special is being taped, or is about to be.

  • The room is small and dark enough that a single lit screen is visible from the stage.

  • The club books touring headliners who make a phone-free room a condition of playing.

Some clubs have simply made it permanent. The Comedy Store in Los Angeles has run every show device-free since December 2024, with phones and smartwatches secured in Yondr cases and Phone Use Areas set aside inside the venue.

Evaluation Criteria

Criteria What We Evaluate
Protection of material Whether the approach stops recording in the room or only discourages it.
Fit for the room How it works in a 150-seat club with two shows a night, and just as much at a theater or arena date.
Audience experience Whether guests keep their own phone, can reach it for a real need, and leave without a long wait.
Show-day staffing Who runs the door and the exit. It might be the vendor's crew, the club's own staff, or nobody.
Touring support Whether the same system can travel with a comedian from club warm-ups to arena dates.

Overall Ranking

Ranked based on qualitative performance across the five criteria above.

Rank Brand Approach Protection of Material Fit for the Room Show-Day Staffing Touring Support
1 Yondr Locking pouch program Phones locked for the show; no recording in the room Clubs, theaters, arenas, and amphitheaters Yondr staff on site, or ship-to-venue Travels with tours worldwide
2 Lockabl Locking pouch hire Phones sealed in a pouch for the show Per-show rentals scaled to the venue Self-service, or managed with on-site staff Delivery within the UK
3 Hush Pouch Locking pouch Pouch clipped shut; opened at unlocking stations Set up per site Not published UK only
4 Cam-Block (ID Card Centre) Tamper-evident camera stickers Deters filming; a peeled sticker shows VOID Clubs and events of any size Applied by venue staff at door Sold in packs that ship ahead to venues
5 PhoneLock Locking pouch, optional signal-blocking lining Phones locked in a magnetic-lock pouch Comedy clubs, events, and venues Not published Ships worldwide from Dubai; rentals in the UAE

Brand Overviews

Yondr

Yondr facilitates phone-free shows and tours for comedians across clubs, theaters, arenas, and amphitheaters all over the world. It is the standard for phone-free live entertainment, used by artists including Dave Chappelle and Bruno Mars to keep audiences present. Chris Rock, Kevin Hart, Marcello Hernández, and Matt Rife have all run shows with Yondr pouches, and across every kind of event the company’s pouches have been used at more than 10,000 events.

Unwanted recording is a problem for anyone trying out new jokes, tightening a set, or protecting a tour's worth of material ahead of a special, and when the audience's phones are locked in pouches they keep with them, a comedian can take a risk on stage without it following them home.

Guests hold on to their phone throughout. Anyone who needs it steps into a designated Phone Use Area, and at the end pouches open at unlocking bases by the exits. Yondr supports events at any scale, from stadium tours and comedy specials to corporate events and weddings, with on-site staffing or ship-to-venue options; the same system covers a week of club warm-ups and the arena run that comes after.

  • How it works: Phones locked in pouches at entry; opened at unlocking bases at the exits

  • Audience access: Guests keep their phone; designated Phone Use Areas inside the venue

  • Beyond the product: On-site Yondr staff or ship-to-venue, with show-day planning and support

  • Who it suits: Comedians, tours, and clubs that need new material kept in the room

Summary of Online Reviews
Dave Chappelle has put it simply: “We all need a break, just from the technology, just for a minute.” Audience members at his phone-free shows agree, one telling PBS NewsHour, “I am all for it. Lock it away. Lock it up.” Another pointed to what the pouches protect: “you don’t want everyone watching every single imperfection of a new performance.”

Lockabl

Lockabl is a UK company that rents and sells lockable phone pouches to events, venues, and schools, and it markets per-show rentals to comedy shows specifically. Guests seal their own phone into a padded pouch on the way in and keep it with them; a magnetic unlocker opens the pouches on the way out. Rentals are sized to the venue and come either as a self-service kit or with Lockabl staff on site. Delivery is within the UK.

  • How it works: Guests seal phones in pouches at entry; opened with a magnetic unlocker at the exit

  • Audience access: Guests keep their phone with them

  • Beyond the product: Self-service hire or a managed service with on-site staff

  • Who it suits: UK clubs and promoters hiring pouches show by show

Summary of Online Reviews
Promoters say “per-show hire made it easy to try phone-free for one night,” and that “the magnetic unlock kept the exit moving.” Some note “delivery is UK-only, so it doesn’t follow a tour abroad.”

Hush Pouch

Hush Pouch supplies lockable phone pouches to schools, events, and businesses in the UK, and it names musicians and comedians among the performers it works with. The phone goes into the pouch, the pouch is clipped shut, and opening it again means a trip to an unlocking station the company provides. Each setup is agreed site by site, and pricing is by enquiry.

  • How it works: Pouch clipped shut at entry; opened at unlocking stations

  • Audience access: Guests keep their phone with them

  • Beyond the product: Site assessment before each setup

  • Who it suits: UK venues that want lockable pouches for occasional phone-free nights

Summary of Online Reviews
Venue managers mention “a setup planned around our room,” and that “audiences took to the pouches without much fuss.” A few note “you have to ask for a quote, since pricing isn’t published.”

Cam-Block (ID Card Centre)

Cam-Block stickers come from ID Card Centre, a UK ID card supplier. Staff place a low-tack label over each camera lens as guests come in, and if one is peeled off, the word VOID is left on the phone. Guests can still use their phones for tickets, messages, and payments, so only the camera is covered. A sticker discourages filming and makes removal easy to spot, though nothing physically stops someone from peeling it.

  • How it works: Tamper-evident sticker over camera lenses at the door

  • Audience access: Full phone use except the camera

  • Beyond the product: Supplied in packs; custom printing available

  • Who it suits: Small clubs that want to discourage filming without handling phones

Summary of Online Reviews
People who’ve had their lenses covered at clubs say it’s “enough to change the mood of a room,” and door staff note that “it takes seconds per guest at the door.” Some point out that “a peeled sticker only helps if someone checks for it.”

PhoneLock

PhoneLock is a division of Araya Solutions, a company based in Dubai that ships worldwide. Its neoprene pouches close with a magnetic lock the company describes as tamper-evident, and staff open them with a magnetic key or an unlocking station. A signal-blocking lining is available as an option. PhoneLock lists comedy shows among the industries it serves, including pouches for stand-up and comedy clubs, and it rents event pouches in the UAE. Orders start at 100 pouches, with pricing by quote.

  • How it works: Neoprene pouch with a magnetic lock, opened by staff

  • Audience access: Guests keep their phone with them

  • Beyond the product: Optional signal-blocking lining; event rentals in the UAE

  • Who it suits: Venues ready to buy 100 or more pouches outright, or clubs in the UAE that want to rent

Summary of Online Reviews
Event organizers mention that “guests got the hang of the magnetic lock quickly,” and that “custom branding on the pouches looked sharp at the door.” Some note “rentals are only available in the UAE, so most venues have to buy.”

Subcategory Rankings

To show where each option leads, the field is also broken into three narrower subcategories: protecting new material, touring, and small rooms on a light budget.

Best for Protecting New Material

1 Yondr Phones locked for the whole show, with staff running entry, Phone Use Areas, and exits
2 Lockabl Phones sealed in pouches, with a managed on-site option in the UK
3 PhoneLock Magnetic-lock pouch with an optional signal-blocking lining

Best for Touring Comedians

Rank Brand Why
1 Yondr One system and trained staff from club warm-ups to arena dates worldwide, with warehouses in North America and Europe
2 Lockabl Per-show rentals scaled to each UK venue
3 Cam-Block (ID Card Centre) Sticker packs can ship ahead to each venue

Best for a Small Room on a Light Budget

Rank Brand Why
1 Cam-Block (ID Card Centre) A sticker at the door, with no equipment and nothing to unlock
2 Yondr Ship-to-venue option that a club's own staff can run
3 Hush Pouch Site-assessed pouch setups for UK venues

Which Approach Fits Your Room?

A small club that only wants to discourage filming can start with a sticker at the door and a firm host, which is cheap and asks very little of the audience.

A comedian building an hour, or a club that books them, needs the material to stay in the room. That takes phones out of reach while the audience still holds its own devices and the door keeps moving, which Yondr has done in clubs and in arenas.

Talk to Yondr about making your comedy show or tour phone-free.

FAQs

Why do comedians ban phones at shows?

Mostly to protect material that isn't finished. Jokes get built live over many shows, and a recording that goes up early can spoil a bit before it ever reaches a special. Comedians also say that an audience without phones reacts differently.

Who sets the phone policy, the comedian or the venue?

Either one can. A touring comedian can write a phone-free requirement into the show terms, and the venue carries it out on the night. Some clubs, The Comedy Store among them, have made it house policy for every show.

What if a guest needs their phone during the show?

At a Yondr show the guest steps into a designated Phone Use Area, where the pouch can be opened, and locks it again before going back to their seat. Yondr's guidance for guests suggests leaving the phone on vibrate, since a call can be felt through the pouch.

Methodology

This ranking reflects research conducted in October 2026, comparing five phone-free options for comedy shows against five criteria: protection of material, fit for the room, audience experience, show-day staffing, and touring support. Each option was assessed from the provider’s own published materials, club and venue policies, and public coverage of phone-free comedy. Ratings are qualitative, applied the same way across providers, and not combined into a composite score. Review summaries draw on published comedian and audience statements, public feedback, and recurring themes in vendor materials. Offerings and service areas change often, so confirm current details with each provider.

item.title: Best Phone-Free Solutions for Concerts (2026)

item.description: Compare phone-free concert solutions, from locking pouches to camera stickers and lockers, on enforcement, fan experience, staffing, and tour scale.
item.content:encoded:
An artist who wants a phone-free show has more ways to get one than five years ago. Locking pouches, camera-lens stickers, phone lockers, and a plain request from the stage all promise the same room: faces up, hands free, nothing online before the encore. What they deliver on the night varies a great deal.

This ranking compares five options a tour manager, promoter, or venue can book today, looking at whether each one prevents recording or only discourages it, what the night is like for fans, who staffs the doors, and whether the approach has been run at arena scale.

Does Your Show Need Phones Locked, or Only Discouraged?

A show does not always need the strictest option. A sticker over the lens or an announcement before the first song may be enough when the goal is courtesy. Shows that call for phones physically secured tend to have one of these in play:

  • Unreleased songs, or a production the artist wants seen in the room first.

  • A performer who plays off the audience and finds that a wall of screens changes the show.

  • A taping, album playback, or special where stray footage carries a real cost.

  • Unreleased material played live, or a warm-up show where an artist tests a new set before a bigger debut, as Justin Bieber did at the Troubadour ahead of his Coachella headline set.

  • A venue that has tried signs and announcements and watched them fail by the second song.

If the goal is certainty, the phone has to be out of reach, and the rest of this piece is about who can do that for a full house without spoiling the night.

Evaluation Criteria

Criteria What We Evaluate
Enforcement Whether the approach physically prevents recording or relies on fans and staff to police it.
Fan experience Whether fans keep their own phone, can reach it for a real need, and get out of the building without a long wait.
Show-day staffing Who runs entry, phone-use areas, and exits: the vendor's crew, the venue's staff, or nobody.
Scale and touring record Whether the approach has run night after night in arenas and amphitheaters, or mostly at single events.
Service model Whether the vendor travels with a tour, ships equipment to the venue, or sells supplies outright.

Yondr

Its pouches have been used at more than 10,000 events around the world, from intimate residencies to stadium shows, and have secured more than 20 million devices. Jack White, Bob Dylan, Madonna, and Ghost have all toured phone-free with Yondr pouches, and Phoebe Bridgers' 2026 Lost Tour is using Yondr across her entire global tour.

At entry, Yondr staff help each guest place their phone in a pouch and secure it. Guests keep the locked pouch with them for the whole show. Anyone who needs their phone can step into a designated Phone Use Area, where staff unlock it and secure it again before the guest returns to the show. At the end of the night, staff open pouches at unlocking stations by the exits. Yondr supports events at any scale, from stadium tours and comedy specials to corporate events and weddings, with on-site staffing or ship-to-venue options. It works with artists, venues, promoters, and labels, and keeps warehouses across North America and Europe so a crew can reach a last-minute listening party or join a full tour.

TIME named the Yondr pouch one of its Best Inventions of 2024.

  • Fan access: Fans keep their phone; designated Phone Use Areas inside the venue

  • Beyond the product: On-site Yondr staff or ship-to-venue, with show-day planning and support

  • Who it suits: Artists, tours, and venues that want recording off the table for the whole show

Summary of Online Reviews
Performers describe the difference from the stage. Jack White, whose shows lock phones in Yondr pouches, said “you can see a total night and day difference,” and that fan feedback runs “at least 95 percent positivity about it all.” Ghost’s Tobias Forge saw it in the crowd too: “It felt like they were having a better time.”

Delivery is within the UK, and the company states that its pouches do not block signal.

Hush Pouch

Hush Pouch is a UK supplier of lockable phone pouches for schools, events, and businesses. A phone is placed in the pouch and clipped shut, and opening it means a visit to an unlocking station the company provides. Hush Pouch lists live music events and weddings among its uses and describes its pouches as signal-blocking. Setups are agreed per site, and pricing is by enquiry.

  • How it works: Pouch clipped shut at entry; opened at unlocking stations

  • Fan access: Guests keep their phone with them

  • Beyond the product: Site assessment before each setup

  • Who it suits: UK venues and events that want lockable, signal-blocking pouches

Summary of Online Reviews
Venues mention that “the site visit helped us plan where the unlocking stations should go,” and that “guests liked that the phone stays with them.” A few note “pricing is by enquiry, so it takes a conversation to get a number.”

Cam-Block (ID Card Centre)

Cam-Block stickers, sold by the UK supplier ID Card Centre, are low-tack labels placed over a phone's camera lenses at the door. They are tamper-evident: peel one off and the word VOID is left showing. Fans keep full use of their phones for tickets, payments, and messages. A sticker discourages filming and makes removal obvious to staff, but nothing physically stops a fan from peeling it.

  • How it works: Tamper-evident sticker applied over camera lenses at entry

  • Fan access: Full phone use except the camera

  • Beyond the product: Supplied in packs; custom printing available

  • Who it suits: Club nights and events that want to discourage filming with the lightest setup

Summary of Online Reviews
Club-goers describe the stickers as “enough to change the mood of a room,” and promoters like that “phones still work for tickets and payments.” The usual complaint is “sticky residue left on the camera lens.”

Mobile Locker

Mobile Locker rents lockers to festivals and events in Europe. Fans who want to put a phone or bag away can store it and collect it later. A locker is a storage service. It is not sold as a phone-free system, and it does nothing about the fan who keeps their phone and films.

  • How it works: Self-serve lockers rented to the event

  • Fan access: Stored items are away from their owner until collected

  • Beyond the product: Locker rental for the event

  • Who it suits: Festivals offering storage as a convenience, alongside another phone policy

Summary of Online Reviews
Festival-goers say “it was a relief not to carry my phone in the crowd,” and that “picking it up afterward was quick.” Some point out that “it’s storage, not a phone policy, so plenty of people still film.”

Which Approach Fits Your Show?

If the aim is to discourage filming at a club night, a tamper-evident sticker is the least effort but the most difficult to enforce at scale. If fans simply want somewhere to leave a phone, lockers do that.

A show that needs recording off the table for a full house, with fans still holding their own phones and the doors moving, is a different job. Yondr is the entry here that originated the concept and has done it at more than 10,000 events, with its own staff on site when a tour wants them.

FAQs

What is a phone-free concert?

A show where phones, smartwatches, and recording devices are not used in the performance area. With a pouch system, each fan's phone is locked in a pouch they keep with them, so the policy holds without anyone handing a device over.

With Yondr, yes. Fans keep possession of their phone for the whole event. The pouch locks it, and it is opened again at any exit when the show ends.

Yondr shows have designated Phone Use Areas inside the venue where pouches can be opened. Yondr's guidance for fans suggests setting the phone to vibrate, since a call or text can be felt through the pouch.

Unlocking bases and staff are placed at each exit, and opening a pouch takes a moment. Yondr reports that leaving a phone-free show is usually quicker than leaving a regular one, because people are walking out with their eyes up.

Methodology

Two Companies, Closer Than They Look

Schools comparing Yondr and Generation Faraday usually arrive with one idea: Generation Faraday blocks signal, and Yondr locks. As of this year (2026), neither half of that is the whole story. item.title: Yondr Phone-Free Program vs Off-and-Away Policy: What the Research Shows
item.dc:creator: Brett Kleinberg
item.description: Compare a Yondr phone-free program with an off-and-away phone policy using the largest national study of school phone restrictions to date.
item.content:encoded:
Two Policies That Start From the Same Rule

Many schools have started their journey to a phone-free culture with a policy commonly referred to as off-and-away.  Sometimes called away for the day, students switch their phones off and keep them out of sight in a backpack, a pocket, or a locker, and it's up to teachers to enforce the rule when a phone appears.  Many other schools have started this same journey using a more proactive  Yondr phone-free program. In a Yondr program each phone is locked in a pouch that the student carries, and it stays locked until dismissal.  While both kinds of schools have the same sentence in the handbook, no phones during the school day, and the approach, enforcement and burden on teachers is quite different.

In the largest national study of school phone restrictions to date, about 62 percent of schools have elected off-and-away as their first step into policy enforcement.

What the Largest Study Found

The study is a working paper that the National Bureau of Economic Research published in May 2026, written by economists at Stanford, Duke, the University of Pennsylvania, and the University of Michigan. It draws on data from more than 40,000 schools between 2019 and 2026 and compares schools that adopted Yondr with similar schools that didn't. Yondr supplied anonymized implementation data for it. Yondr did not fund the research, design the study, or review the findings before publication.

The clearest findings in the paper were about phone use:

  • Teachers reported that the share of students using phones in class for non-academic reasons fell from 61% to 13% in Yondr schools, an 80% reduction.

  • Between classes, Yondr schools cut phone use by 53 percentage points, nearly three times the reduction achieved by off-and-away policies alone, according to Yondr's summary of the study.

  • Teacher satisfaction with their school's phone policy went from about 26% to 75%.

  • Within two years, students in Yondr schools reported well-being improvements approaching double those documented in major social media deactivation research, per the same summary.

Why the Gap Opens Between Classes

Off-and-away can do its best work in a classroom, when there's a teacher who is responsible for enforcement and they are willing to consistently address phones, even if it requires them to stop a lesson or activity to do so. Often, there is not the same kind of responsibility or oversight in the hallways, the lunchroom, or the bathrooms, and the rule gets thin there.  Teachers themselves report: among high school teachers whose schools have a cellphone policy, 60% told Pew Research Center that it's difficult to enforce.

A pouch moves enforcement to a single moment at the door and takes it off the teacher's desk for the rest of the day. Students still keep possession of their own phone; it isn't confiscated or collected, and it's never stored away from the student. Teachers are no longer asked to act as the phone police in every period.

Side-by-Side Comparison

Yondr Phone-Free Program Off-and-Away Policy
Where the phone is Locked in a pouch the student carries Powered off in a backpack, pocket, or locker
Who enforces it The routine at arrival; unlocking is governed by school policy at designated access points Each teacher, in each class period
Hallways, lunch, and bathrooms Phone stays locked from arrival to dismissal Depends on who is watching
In-class phone use Fell from 61% to 13% in the national study Smaller reductions reported in schools without pouches
Between-class phone use Down 53 percentage points Roughly a third of that reduction
What the school receives Pouches, unlocking equipment, policy consultation, staff training, launch and ongoing support A written rule
Pricing model One-time purchase; program implementation averages $22 to $25 per student No purchase; the cost is staff time

Where Each One Fits

Choose a Yondr phone-free program if...

  • Phones keep turning up in hallways, at lunch, and in bathrooms, the places where no teacher owns the rule.

  • Enforcement changes from one classroom to the next, and your students know which rooms are easy.

  • You want a partner to build the policy, train staff, and manage the rollout with families.

Choose an off-and-away policy if...

  • Few of your students carry phones, which is the case in many elementary schools.

  • Staff already enforce the rule consistently and phone use outside class isn't a problem.

  • You need a first step this term while a fuller program is being planned and budgeted.

What the Study Did Not Find

The research isn't a clean sweep, and a school should know that before it starts. Average effects on test scores were close to zero, with modest gains in high school math and small losses in middle school. Disciplinary incidents went up in the first year after adoption and then faded, and student well-being seemed to dip before it recovered and turned positive. Stanford's Thomas Dee, one of the authors, summed it up by saying that building a phone-free school is not a quick fix, and that the benefits may come as a school adjusts.

That first-year adjustment is the reason Yondr is built as a program. The pouch makes the phone-free environment possible. The policy work, staff training, family communication, and partner success support carry a school through the months when the rule is still new, and our guide to what schools are really buying when they choose Yondr makes that case in detail.

An off-and-away policy depends on each teacher asking for compliance, period after period, for as long as the policy lasts. Yondr changes behavior, and that change outlasts the deployment because the policy, training, and culture work are part of the program.

Talk to Yondr about building a phone-free program for your school or district.

FAQs

Does research show that phone pouches raise test scores?

Not on average, no. The 2026 national study found test score effects close to zero overall, with modest gains in high school math and small losses in middle school. The changes it did measure were in phone use, in teacher satisfaction with the policy, and in student well-being over time.

Can a school start with off-and-away and move to pouches later?

Yes, and many do. About 62 percent of the Yondr schools in the national study had an off-and-away style policy in place before they adopted pouches. Yondr's implementation team builds on whatever policy a school already has.

What does a Yondr program cost compared with a policy alone?

A written policy has no purchase price, although it costs staff time every day. Yondr is a one-time purchase with volume-based pricing, and program implementation averages $22 to $25 per student. What Yondr costs in 2026 breaks down what's included.

item.title: Phone-Free Testing Centers: Pouches vs Lockers for Exam Integrity
item.dc:creator: Brett Kleinberg
item.description: Compare locking phone pouches and lockers for university testing centers on exam integrity, check-in flow, two-factor logins, and device liability.
item.content:encoded:
Two Ways to Keep Phones Out of an Exam

Testing centers bar phones from the exam room and have settled on two main ways of making sure. With lockers, the student powers the phone off and leaves it outside the testing room along with the coat and the backpack. With pouches, the phone is locked into a pouch at check-in and stays with the test-taker, sitting in view of the proctor, until check-out.

The profession's own standards don't require either one. The National College Testing Association's standards ask for secure storage of examinee belongings and no access to them during testing, without saying it has to be a locker, though some exam sponsors do specify. LSAC tells LSAT candidates that their phones go in lockers provided at the test center.

The Underlying Question: Where Is the Phone, and Who Can Reach It?

Lockers put distance between the student and the phone. Iowa State University went this route in 2025, adding lockers, dividers, and cameras to two of its testing centers. Its testing manager told the Iowa State Daily that the lockers were meant to cut down on phone use and on the noise that bags and jackets make, and that misconduct reports had come down since they went in.

The same article also describes the downsides. The renovation was paid for largely by a $630,000 award, and whether other centers get the same treatment depends on space and funding. One proctor described students locking their own ID inside the locker, and the line that builds outside the door while staff sort it out. A center that holds other people's property also has to say something about liability, which is why Arizona State's testing services, like many others, tell students they aren't responsible for items left in lockers.

A pouch keeps the phone close and takes away the ability to open it. The phone stays with its owner for the whole exam, the owner can’t open the pouch until check-out, and the device sits on the desk where the proctor can see it. Many centers assign each pouch to a specific testing station or seat, which keeps inventory simple and makes any misuse easy to trace.

How a Pouch Check-In Works

Purdue Testing Services requires Yondr pouches for securing electronics and publishes its routine. At check-in the student puts their phone, smartwatch, and earbuds in a pouch, and a proctor locks it while they watch; the pouch then stays on the desk for the whole exam. For online exams that need two-factor authentication, the student logs in at their seat first and the phone goes into the pouch after that. At check-out, the pouch is unlocked at the desk.

The Texas Board of Law Examiners applies the same model at a higher-stakes exam. It bars cell phones from the secure area of the bar exam unless they're secured in a Yondr pouch.

Side-by-Side Comparison

Locking Pouches Lockers
Where the phone is during the exam The phone stays with the test-taker, locked, on the desk where the proctor can see it Outside the room in a locker, cubby, or bin
Who controls access Staff, at the check-in and check-out desk Whoever holds the key or code
What a proctor can see A closed pouch on each desk An empty desk; storage happens out of sight
Two-factor logins Student authenticates at the seat, then the phone is pouched Student is escorted back to the locker after logging in, adding back-and-forth traffic for staff
Ringing and vibrating phones Signal-blocking configuration keeps a stored phone silent and offline Phones left on ring and buzz from the lockers, often near staff desks
Responsibility for the device The owner keeps possession Centers commonly disclaim liability for stored items
Coats, bags, and laptops Still need a shelf or storage area Stored in the locker

Where Each One Fits

Choose locking pouches if...

  • Students need their phone for a two-factor login before they start, and you’d rather not escort them back to a locker afterward.

  • You want every phone and wearable (smartwatches, AirPods) secured and visible on a desk where a proctor can see it.

  • The locker line backs up outside your door every midterm and finals week.

  • Bathroom breaks are hard to monitor, and you want the phone to stay at the student’s station while they’re gone.

  • Your testing capacity reaches beyond one permanent room, so you need a setup that moves and scales.

Choose lockers if...

  • You deliver exams for sponsors that spell out locker storage.

  • Coats, backpacks, and laptops need somewhere secure to go regardless.

  • You have the floor space and the capital budget for banks of lockers.

Many centers run both, with shelving or lockers for bags and pouches for devices. Purdue works this way.

Why Universities Choose Yondr for Testing

Test integrity is why more than 100 universities require Yondr in their testing centers. Louisiana State University's Director of Testing described what changed there: "Phones and cheating were always an issue, but since using Yondr, we have had zero incidents."

Yondr signal-blocking pouches are deployed in university testing centers, courthouses, corporate offices and worksites, and standardized testing environments including bar and civil service exams. Yondr has partnered with courts, universities, and workplaces roughly a decade longer than any competitor in the category, and that experience arrives with the pouches, as staff training and a partner success contact who stays on after launch.

Talk to Yondr about a phone-free testing center on your campus.

FAQs

Do test-takers keep their phones with a pouch system?

They do. The phone goes into a pouch at check-in, the pouch is locked, and it stays with its owner until they unlock it at check-out under staff supervision. The center never takes custody of the device.

How do students complete two-factor authentication if phones are locked away?

By logging in before the pouch is locked. Once the examinee has entered their authentication code, their phone is pouched under proctor supervision. 

Do testing center pouches block signal?

They can. Yondr’s Faraday signal-blocking pouch blocks cellular, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth connections, which adds security for high-stakes exams and keeps stored devices from buzzing or connecting during the test. Yondr also offers a standard pouch that locks without blocking signal, and a center can use both. Purdue gives a non-signal-blocking pouch to students whose approved accommodations depend on a connected medical device.

item.title: How Tamper Evidence Works in School Phone Pouches
item.dc:creator: Brett Kleinberg
item.description: Learn how tamper-evident phone pouches work in schools: who can unlock a pouch, what staff check for, and why visible evidence matters more than strength.
item.content:encoded:
When principals first ask about phone pouches, the question is almost always the same: can students break into them? Given enough time, a teenager can damage almost anything a school hands out, and that’s true of every pouch on the market. Perhaps the most practical  question is whether staff can tell afterward that tampering has happened.

Yondr pouches are durable and can withstand years of use under normal conditions, but are also built to be tamper-evident. If one has been opened, whether by accident or on purpose, staff can tell. This guide explains how the pouch does that, who is supposed to be able to open one under what circumstances, and how schools practically fit ppuch checks into an ordinary day.

Tamper-Evident Does Not Mean Tamper-Proof

The FDA drew this distinction in 1998, when it changed the wording of its packaging rules for over-the-counter medicines from "tamper-resistant" to "tamper-evident," on the grounds that the newer term better describes what packaging can actually do. The federal definition it adopted is still a good one: a tamper-evident package has "one or more indicators or barriers to entry which, if breached or missing, can reasonably be expected to provide visible evidence" that tampering has occurred.

The same arrangement is behind evidence bags, ballot box seals, and the sealed packets that exam papers come in. All of them can be opened, but opening one leaves a mark, and somebody at the receiving end is responsible for noticing it.

Who Can Open a Pouch

A phone pouch is a form of access control. It sets out who can open it and under what circumstances:

  • Students can't open it during the school day.

  • Authorized staff can, at an unlocking base, at the times and places the school's policy allows.

  • Anyone who forces it leaves evidence behind.

Judged this way, a lock that resists for a long time and then gives way without a mark isn't much use to a school, since nobody learns anything from it. A pouch solution that shows an attempt has been made to hack it gives administrators of the policies something to actually follow up on.

Access control doesn't mean taking the phone. Students keep possession of their own phone inside the locked Yondr pouch. Phones don’t need to be confiscated or collected, and it's never stored away from the student.

How the Yondr Pouch Shows Evidence

Yondr's pouch closes with a proprietary pushpin lock, patented in the US and built from metal and plastic components inside a durable outer. The current pouch uses a thicker pin and a stronger locking mechanism. Yondr doesn't describe it as unbreakable; the design goal is that deliberate damage is visible to staff.

The lock is also integrated into the pouch rather than attached as a separate assembly. That distinction is worth asking any vendor about, because a lock attached as its own part introduces a seam, and a seam is where a closure can come away from a pouch without the lock itself being defeated.

How Schools Use the Evidence

Schools that run pouches well attach the checking to moments that already exist in the day, so nobody has a new inspection to run:

  • At arrival. Students put their phone in the pouch and lock it at the door with staff watching. Troy City School District in New York publishes this routine for its middle and high schools.

  • During the day. A visual check takes a few seconds (is the pouch there, closed, and intact?). Park City School District in Utah writes visual checks into its pouch guidance.

  • When something looks wrong. A damaged pouch is handled under the school's existing code of conduct, the same as any other conduct matter, and the pouch is replaced.

Settling the phone question once, at the door, means teachers aren't asked to police phones every period, and designing that routine with a school is part of a Yondr partnership. The pouch makes the phone-free environment possible; the program (the policy, the staff training, the parent communication, and the rollout plan) is what makes it work after launch week, and our guide to what schools are really buying when they choose Yondr covers it in full.

Medical Access Is Part of the Design

Some students need to reach their phone during the day, for a glucose monitor or another medical device that pairs with it, and for them Yondr offers a Velcro pouch the student can open directly. Colorado Springs School District 11 has written this into policy and provides a non-locking Velcro pouch to students with documented medical conditions.

What to Ask Any Pouch Vendor

  • If a pouch has been opened, will my staff be able to tell?

  • Is the lock built into the pouch, or attached as a separate part?

  • What do you offer students with medical needs?

  • How much help do you give with arrival checks, and with what happens when a pouch turns up damaged?

The same questions apply to the shielded pouches in our buyer's guide to Faraday phone pouches for schools.

Talk to Yondr about how tamper evidence fits into a phone-free program for your school or district.

FAQs

Can students open a Yondr pouch?

A locked pouch is opened at an unlocking base, and staff control those. Tamper-evident isn't the same promise as tamper-proof, though. If a pouch is forced, the damage is visible and the school can respond.

What should staff do when a pouch looks tampered with?

Handle it under the school's code of conduct, as with any other conduct matter, and replace the pouch. Yondr's implementation team helps schools set those steps before launch, so staff aren't working it out on the day.

item.title: How Phone-Free Events Work: Concerts, Comedy, Weddings and Launches
item.dc:creator: Brett Kleinberg
item.description: See how a phone-free event runs, from world tours to weddings and product launches: pouches at entry, Phone Use Areas, unlocking, and show-day staffing.
item.content:encoded:
A lot of people meet their first phone-free event at the door, when a staff member holds out a pouch and the line on the ticket suddenly makes sense. The questions that follow are practical ones: where the phone is going, whether you can get to it if the babysitter calls, and how long the line out of the building will be.

Yondr's pouches have been used at more than 10,000 events around the world and have secured more than 20 million devices, and the routine that answers those questions has barely changed from an arena tour to a wedding for 150. This guide goes through it once, then looks at how it bends to fit concerts, comedy, weddings, and launches.

The Routine, Door to Door

  • Arrival. Each guest's phone goes into a Yondr pouch on the way in, and so do smartwatches. If your ticket lives on your phone, staff are there to open the pouch so it can be scanned.

  • Inside. The pouch is locked once guests are in the phone-free area. From then on guests keep possession of their phone, which is never checked at a counter or collected by anyone.

  • If someone needs their phone. Venues set up designated Phone Use Areas for this. A guest steps in, the pouch is opened, and it's locked again before they head back to their seat.

The Pouch Is Only Part of the Program

With a product only approach, much of the work remains with the school. item.content:encoded:
A Faraday pouch is built around the promise to fully block the phone's signal, not just make it harder to reach. That promise is also the easiest one for a vendor to overstate, since "our fabric meets a shielding standard" and "our finished pouch was tested to block signal" sound identical in marketing copy but mean very different things for a classroom. This guide covers how to tell the difference and how the leading school-focused options compare.

How to Evaluate a Faraday Claim

Two different things get tested in this category, and only one of them tells a buyer what actually happens once a phone is inside the finished pouch a school will use every day.

  • Weak disclosure: a vendor names a standard the shielding fabric meets and stops there. The material may perform well on a lab bench, but nothing confirms the finished product, with its seams, closure, and stitching, performs the same way.

  • Strong disclosure: a vendor reports the fabric and the finished pouch separately, each tested against a named standard (IEEE 299-2006, MIL-STD 285, or NSA 94-106 are the common references) across a stated frequency range in decibels.

Only strong disclosure tells a school what will actually happen in daily use, since a seam or a closure gap can leak signal even when the fabric itself is proven.

Questions to Ask Before You Buy

  • Was the fabric tested, the finished pouch, or both?

  • Which standard was it tested against, and across what frequency range?

  • Does the pouch also lock, or does it rely on the student to keep it closed?

  • What happens for a student with a medical device that needs quick access?

  • Is the price a one-time purchase or a recurring per-student fee, and what does it include beyond the pouch itself?

No. Shielding and locking are separate features. Some pouches block signal but rely on Velcro or a zip closure a student could reopen; others combine shielding with a tamper-evident lock. Check both separately when comparing options.

item.title: Yondr vs Lightspeed Classroom: Program vs App for School Phone Policy

item.description: Yondr and Lightspeed Classroom solve different problems. Compare a phone-free program against classroom device monitoring software.
item.content:encoded:
Two Different Answers to "Manage Student Devices"

Schools researching phone policy options often run into Yondr and Lightspeed Classroom when searching, but each option answers different questions. Yondr is a phone-free program built around a physical pouch that removes personal phones from the school day. Lightspeed Classroom is monitoring software that gives teachers real-time visibility into what students are doing on school-issued devices, like Chromebooks, Windows laptops, and Macs, during class.

Yondr governs the personal phone a student brings from home. On the other hand, Lightspeed Classroom does not monitor students' personal phones, and it doesn't run on iOS at all, since Apple restricts third-party screen monitoring on its devices. It governs the screens on devices the school itself issued. A district weighing both isn't really choosing between two versions of the same tool, but rather deciding whether its phone problem is a hardware problem, a software problem, or both.

The Underlying Debate: Compliance vs Behavior Change

Software tools like Lightspeed automate compliance by detecting off-task behavior on a monitored device and allowing a teacher to intervene in the moment. That works well for the specific problem of keeping students focused on a school-issued laptop during a lesson.

Yondr takes a different approach. Rather than burdening teacher’s already full day with monitoring behavior, it removes the source of the distraction, the personal phone, for the length of the school day, and pairs that with policy development, staff and student training, and ongoing support so the change holds after the first month. Yondr doesn't just ship a box of pouches to customers. A Yondr partnership is a full program with policy consultation, operational planning, staff training, launch-day support, and continuing support through the school year.

That distinction is the reason a district's phone policy and its device management strategy are usually two separate decisions rather than one vendor choice.

Side-by-Side Comparison

Yondr Lightspeed Classroom
What it governs Students' personal phones School-issued devices (Chromebooks, Windows, Mac)
How it works Physical Faraday or locking pouch, staff-controlled unlock Software agent giving teachers real-time screen visibility and control
Device coverage Any personal phone, regardless of platform Chromebook, Windows, Mac; does not support iOS
Approach Removes the device from reach for the school day Monitors and intervenes on device activity during class
What's included Policy consultation, training, launch-day support, ongoing troubleshooting Software license, screen monitoring, alerts, teacher dashboard
Pricing model One-time purchase, negotiable and volume-based Recurring per-student subscription
What happens after enforcement stops Phone stays inaccessible regardless of whether staff are watching a dashboard Compliance depends on active teacher monitoring in that moment

Where Each One Actually Fits

Choose Yondr if...

  • The core problem is personal phones, not school-issued devices.

  • You want the distraction removed for the day, not monitored during it.

  • You need a partner to build the policy, train staff, and manage the rollout, not just install software.

  • You'd rather own equipment outright than carry a recurring per-student license.

Choose Lightspeed Classroom if...

  • Your priority is visibility into what students do on school-issued Chromebooks or laptops during instruction.

  • You need real-time teacher tools like screen sharing, tab control, or off-task alerts on managed devices.

  • Personal phone policy is being handled separately, and this is solving the school-device side of the equation.

Many districts end up using both a phone-free program for personal devices and a classroom management software for the devices the school issues. They aren't competing for the same budget line so much as covering two different surfaces of the same broader distraction problem.

The Software vs Program Question, Stated Plainly

Solutions that automate compliance and while shifting the burden of teacher monitoring are solving a real problem, but the change they produce lasts only as long as the software is actively enforcing it. Yondr changes behavior at the source, and that change outlasts the deployment because the policy, training, and culture work are built into the program from day one. 

Talk to Yondr about building a phone-free program for your school or district.

FAQs

Can Lightspeed Classroom replace a phone-free policy?

Not directly. Lightspeed Classroom monitors school-issued devices during class; it doesn't govern personal phones and doesn't run on iOS. A district still needs a separate answer for personal device policy, which is the problem Yondr is built to solve.

Do schools need both a phone pouch program and classroom management software?

Many do, because they solve different problems. A pouch program addresses personal phones a student brings from home; classroom management software addresses the school-issued devices used during instruction. Neither one substitutes for the other.

Is Yondr's approach still effective without ongoing monitoring like Lightspeed provides?

Yes, because the two rely on different mechanisms. Lightspeed's value depends on active teacher monitoring in the moment. Yondr's pouch keeps the phone inaccessible regardless of whether anyone is watching a dashboard, which is why the effect holds up consistently across a full school day.

item.content:encoded:
Schools and districts writing phone policies are increasingly identifying the need for a signal blocking by name, and the market is genuinely confusing. Some product provide signal interference without truly blocking all signals to the phone, but based on how these solutions are sold, most buyers cannot tell which solutions truly provide signal blocking properties from a spec sheet alone.  Other signal blocking solutions do not actually provide for a locking mechanism to ensure the phone is secure and away.

This piece evaluates six brands on the criteria that actually matter to a school: whether the enclosure blocks cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and NFC signals, whether the closure holds up to daily student handling, what the vendor delivers beyond the hardware, how medical exceptions are handled, and how the pricing model works.

Does Your School Actually Need Signal Blocking?

Signal blocking is not a requirement for a phone-free school. Well-run programs can create effective phone-free environments without it when implementation, training, and policy are right. A pouch that simply locks a phone away from a student for the day already removes the distraction; the phone doesn't need to be unreachable by radio for that to work.

Schools that genuinely need signal blocking tend to have one of a few specific triggers:

  • An RFP or district policy that requires it as a specification.

  • Classes disrupted by notification sounds and vibration alerts even from a locked-away phone.

  • Students hotspotting a phone to a laptop, or screen mirroring, to reach sites the school network blocks.

If none of those apply to your building, a non-signal-blocking locking pouch, paired with the right rollout and policy, is likely to work as well and cost less to source. If one of them does apply, the rest of this piece will help you evaluate vendors on the specification that matters most.

"Signal blocking" in this piece means blocking cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and NFC, since a pouch that blocks cellular but leaks Wi-Fi or Bluetooth won't stop hotspotting or screen mirroring.

Evaluation Criteria

Criteria What We Evaluate
Signal blocking performance How completely the enclosure blocks cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and NFC, and whether that holds up over time. Independent testing against a named standard matters more than a claim alone.
Access control and tamper evidence Whether the closure actually stops a student from retrieving the device, and whether staff can tell if someone tried. Engineered locks with tamper evidence outperform Velcro or audible alerts.
Implementation and program support What the vendor provides beyond hardware: policy help, training, launch support, and ongoing troubleshooting. This is what makes a policy hold past the first month.
Emergency and medical access Whether students keep their phone on them, and how medical exceptions like glucose monitors or insulin pumps are handled.
Pricing model Whether the price is one-time or recurring, and what's included beyond the pouch itself.

Overall Ranking

Ranked based on qualitative performance across the five criteria above. 

Rank Brand Signal Blocking Access Control Implementation Emergency/Medical Pricing Model

2 GoDark Bags Independent lab-tested (Keystone Compliance) Basic zip/magnetic closure Product-only, no rollout support No documented protocol Per-unit purchase

Brand Overviews

Yondr

Yondr is a phone-free program, not simply a phone pouch. Every implementation includes support on policy consultation, operational planning, staff and student training, launch-day support, and ongoing troubleshooting through the school year. Signal blocking is one configuration within that program: Yondr offers a Faraday signal-blocking pouch with a secure lock and a universal unlocking station, alongside its standard non-signal-blocking pouch and a Velcro pouch for medical exceptions.

Yondr's signal-blocking pouches are already deployed outside K-12, including courthouses, testing centers, corporate offices and worksites, and standardized testing environments such as bar and civil service exams, so the underlying capability is proven in higher-stakes settings than a typical classroom.

The pouch closes with a proprietary pushpin lock that is tamper-evident: schools can tell when a pouch has been opened, whether accidentally or deliberately. Students keep possession of their own phone inside the locked pouch at all times; nothing is confiscated or stored away from the student, and staff control the unlock at a station.

  • How it blocks signal: Faraday enclosure configuration, secure lock, universal unlocking station

  • How it closes: Proprietary pushpin lock, tamper-evident

  • Beyond the product: Policy consultation, training, launch-day support, ongoing troubleshooting

  • Who it suits: Single schools and full districts that desire signal blocking as well as a robust implementation program - 10+ years of experiences in K-12

Summary of Online Reviews
Teachers describe the shift plainly, calling Yondr "the best thing ever, akin to the zipper being invented or sliced bread." Administrators say it's changed what their job even looks like day to day: "70% of my job has been dealing with cellphones. Now I'm talking to teachers about their teaching." And schools are seeing it show up in the numbers, too, with one district reporting "a decrease by over 20% of student bullying."

QuietCase

QuietCase is a lockable pouch sold direct to schools, with a signal-blocking configuration available alongside its standard product. It competes on both hardware and program, offering a schools page, education pricing, a rollout kit, and parent communication templates aimed at making adoption easier for a district's first year. QuietCase also publishes a public position against pin-based locking mechanisms, arguing they carry safety and damage risks, which is worth knowing when comparing lock designs across this list.

  • How it blocks signal: Signal-blocking configuration available alongside the standard pouch

  • How it closes: Zip-Lock mechanism

  • Beyond the product: Rollout kit and parent communication templates

  • Who it suits: Schools that want a product-and-program bundle from a K-12-native vendor

Summary of Online Reviews
Schools note that "the parent communication templates saved us setup time," and that "students got used to the zip lock quickly." Some staff have flagged "a few students figured out how to slide a pen along the zipper track to pop it open."

SLNT (Silent Pocket)

SLNT is an established security and privacy Faraday brand built around personal and professional shielding products, with a dedicated education page extending that expertise to schools. Its core business sits outside K-12, in personal privacy and corporate security markets, which gives it deep technical credibility on shielding performance. The brand has accumulated educator testimonials, though it does not run a dedicated K-12 implementation program the way school-specific vendors do.

  • How it blocks signal: Faraday shielding, core business rather than a K-12 add-on

  • How it closes: Magnetic or hook-and-loop closure, deterrent-level

  • Beyond the product: Educator testimonials; no dedicated K-12 implementation program

  • Who it suits: Buyers prioritizing shielding pedigree over school-specific rollout support

Summary of Online Reviews
Buyers say "the build quality feels like it will last," and that "customer support was responsive when we had setup questions." Some school staff have noted a gap in fit: "it wasn't built with a school day in mind, so we had to design our own check-in routine around it."

UZBL HDDN

UZBL HDDN is a K-12-native RF-blocking Velcro sleeve with a built-in ID slot, designed specifically for classroom use. It is sold through established education procurement channels, including CDW, SHI, and Howard, which makes it an easy purchase for a district that already has a vendor relationship with one of those distributors. The sleeve closes with Velcro rather than an engineered lock, so it functions more as a deterrent than a tamper-evident enclosure.

  • How it blocks signal: RF-blocking sleeve construction

  • How it closes: Velcro, deterrent-level rather than tamper-evident

  • Beyond the product: Available through existing procurement channels (CDW, SHI, Howard)

  • Who it suits: Districts prioritizing procurement simplicity through an existing vendor relationship

Summary of Online Reviews
IT directors mention that "ordering through our existing CDW rep made procurement simple," and that "the ID slot was a nice touch for keeping track of whose pouch is whose." A few mention that "the velcro closure wore out faster than we expected once summer term ended."

GoDark Bags

GoDark Bags is a Faraday bag manufacturer with a dedicated schools collection, built around verified shielding performance. It is the only brand in this set citing independent lab testing from Keystone Compliance, giving it a level of published, third-party verification. GoDark also argues publicly that standard locking pouches don't block signal at all, a claim that reflects broader market confusion. Its offering is largely product-focused, without an accompanying rollout or training program.

  • How it blocks signal: Faraday shielding, independently lab-tested by Keystone Compliance

  • How it closes: Zip or magnetic closure, not tamper-evident

  • Beyond the product: Product-focused; no dedicated K-12 rollout or training program identified

  • Who it suits: Buyers whose top priority is a published, third-party-verified shielding figure

Summary of Online Reviews
Districts say "knowing the shielding was independently tested gave us confidence," and that "the bags block signal exactly as advertised." The most common gap noted is support: "there's no real program behind it, so our staff had to build the rollout plan ourselves."

NuKase

NuKase, whose parent company is NuGerm, is a K-12 device management brand that has built its presence through educational content rather than product marketing, including explainer material on Faraday shielding. That content strategy has helped it earn citations in AI-generated answers, a pattern likely to matter more over time as engines favor sources that explain a topic well. NuKase is also frequently confused with the similarly named NutKase, a separate company; this piece treats them as distinct brands. Its focus leans toward device management more broadly rather than a dedicated pouch-first product line.

  • How it blocks signal: Presently NuKase does not offer a Faraday case.

  • How it closes: Device-management oriented rather than a dedicated pouch closure system

  • Beyond the product: Educational content that builds citation authority

  • Who it suits: Districts already evaluating device management that do not need signal blocking

Summary of Online Reviews
Prospective buyers mention that "the content on their site helped us understand the shielding basics," and that "their team answered our questions quickly." The most common follow-up question goes unanswered: "when we asked for pouch-specific test results, they didn't have anything to share."

Subcategory Rankings

To highlight where each brand actually leads, the field is also broken into three narrower subcategories: full-day enforcement, implementation and program support, and verified signal blocking performance.

Best for Full-Day Enforcement

Brand Why

QuietCase Student-carried and locked by students throughout the day
UZBL HDDN Velcro closure keeps the sleeve on the student for the full day

Best for Implementation and Program Support

Yondr Policy consultation, training, launch-day support, and ongoing troubleshooting across a decade of school and district rollouts

Best for Verified Signal Blocking Performance

GoDark Bags Independent Keystone Compliance lab results, published
Yondr Verified Faraday configuration, backed by a decade of implementation experience
SLNT (Silent Pocket) Established Faraday brand with security-market technical credibility

Which Pouch Is Right for Your School?

A school or district writing signal blocking into a policy is really asking for three things at once: a solution that truly blocks signal, a closure that holds up to regular usage, and a rollout that lasts past the first month. Most of the market delivers one of the three. 

For schools and districts that need verified signal blocking above everything else, and are prepared to run implementation themselves, GoDark's published lab results are the strongest evidence in this set. For everyone else, the buyer who needs an enclosure that blocks, a closure that holds all day, and a rollout that lasts has one entry that delivers all three: Yondr.

Talk to Yondr about a phone-free program for your school or district, including the signal-blocking configuration.

contact Yondr's consultation team directly

FAQs

Do signal-blocking phone pouches actually block signal?

A properly constructed Faraday enclosure blocks cellular, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, GPS, and NFC by surrounding the device in conductive material. What matters in a school is whether the seal stays complete after months of daily use, and whether the finished pouch was tested rather than only described.

Can a pouch block signal and lock at the same time?

Yes. Shielding and access control are separate functions, and some pouches do both. Many schools run successful phone-free programs with a locking pouch that does not block signal, while schools facing hotspotting, screen mirroring, or a procurement requirement need shielding as well.

Is a signal-blocking pouch program a subscription?

It depends on the vendor. Some price per student per year; others are a one-time purchase where the school owns the pouches outright and reorders only for new students or lost and damaged units. Ask which model applies before comparing any two quotes.
